params.question: According to the Cruse and Foord concept explained in this module, which combination of factors determines whether a surgical wound becomes infected?

answers.text: The wound classification grade and the duration of surgery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Wound classification and operative duration are relevant risk factors, but the Cruse and Foord concept specifically frames infection as a balance between the bacterial challenge (dose multiplied by virulence) and the host's defences.

answers.text: Bacterial dose and virulence relative to host resistance

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The Cruse and Foord concept states that infection develops when the bacterial challenge — dose multiplied by virulence — overwhelms the patient's systemic and local defences.

answers.text: The type of suture material used and the choice of prophylactic antibiotic

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Suture material and antibiotic choice are management decisions. The Cruse and Foord concept describes pathogenesis: the balance of dose multiplied by virulence versus host resistance.

answers.text: Patient age and the anatomical site of the incision

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Age can weaken host resistance and anatomical site affects local factors, but the concept frames these within the broader balance of bacterial challenge versus total host resistance — not as the balance itself.

overallFeedback.feedback: Infection risk, per the Cruse and Foord concept, is the balance between bacterial dose × virulence and host resistance. All other factors feed into one side of this balance.
The Cruse and Foord concept captures the fundamental pathogenesis: infection follows when dose multiplied by virulence overwhelms host resistance, both systemic and local.

interactions.label: In the context of necrotising fasciitis, why is the emphasis placed on pain out

params.question: In the context of necrotising fasciitis, why is the emphasis placed on pain out of proportion to visible signs as the key early warning, rather than crepitus or skin necrosis?

answers.text: Crepitus is unreliable because it also occurs in many benign wound conditions

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Crepitus in a wound is not a benign finding — it indicates gas in the tissues and is highly suggestive of necrotising infection. The reason it is not the key early sign is that it appears late in the disease course.

answers.text: Skin necrosis is seen only in gas gangrene, not in necrotising fasciitis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Necrotising fasciitis does cause skin necrosis — it is in the name. The point is that visible necrosis is a late sign; by the time it appears, the infection has spread extensively along fascial planes.

answers.text: Crepitus and skin necrosis are late signs — delaying until they appear reduces the chance of successful debridement

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. By the time crepitus and skin necrosis become apparent, the infection has spread widely along fascial planes, making adequate debridement more difficult and mortality significantly higher.

answers.text: Pain out of proportion indicates the infection has already reached the bloodstream, triggering sepsis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The disproportionate pain results from destruction of tissue along fascial planes, not from bloodstream invasion per se. The emphasis is on timing: pain appears before the late, ominous signs, giving the surgeon a window to act.

overallFeedback.feedback: Crepitus and skin necrosis are late findings in necrotising fasciitis. By the time they develop, the infection has spread extensively. Recognising disproportionate pain early is the key to timely, life-saving debridement.

Pain out of proportion to the visible wound appears early, before crepitus and necrosis. Recognising this sign promptly triggers the life-saving decision to operate — waiting for late signs costs lives.

params.question: The 55-year-old diabetic patient in the opening scenario developed a surgical-site infection after emergency surgery. Applying the pathogenesis model, which factor most directly tipped the balance in favour of infection?

answers.text: Emergency surgery was performed after hours, increasing contamination risk

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Emergency surgery can increase the bacterial challenge, but the narration specifically identifies the patient's diabetes as the factor that weakened his immune defences and tipped the Cruse and Foord balance.

answers.text: The surgical team did not administer prophylactic antibiotics before incision

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Prophylactic antibiotics are a management strategy for prevention, not part of the pathogenesis model itself. The narration attributes this infection to diabetes compromising host resistance.

answers.text: A highly virulent organism colonised the wound at the time of injury

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Organism virulence is one side of the Cruse and Foord balance, but the narration identifies diabetes as weakening the host resistance side, making the patient susceptible even to Staphylococcus aureus — the commonest cause.

answers.text: Diabetes impaired his systemic immune defences, reducing host resistance

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Diabetes weakens systemic immune defences — a key host factor in the Cruse and Foord balance. This reduced resistance allowed a surgical-site infection to develop from Staphylococcus aureus, the most common causative organism.

overallFeedback.feedback: The pathogenesis model identifies three forces: pathogen, host, and local environment. The narration specifically identified diabetes as the factor that weakened this patient's systemic host resistance, tipping the balance.

Diabetes impairs systemic host resistance, tipping the Cruse and Foord balance in favour of infection. This illustrates why optimising host factors — nutrition, glycaemic control, immunological status — is central to prevention.
